title: English Wikipedia article: Abstract algebra
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":19616384,"ns":0,"title":"Abstract algebra","extract":"In mathematics, more specifically algebra, abstract algebra or modern algebra is the study of algebraic structures, which are sets with specific operations acting on their elements. Algebraic structures include groups, rings, fields, modules, vector spaces, lattices, and algebras over a field.","description":"Branch of mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: General topology
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":178649,"ns":0,"title":"General topology","extract":"In mathematics, general topology (or point set topology) is the branch of topology that deals with the basic set-theoretic definitions and constructions used in topology. It is the foundation of most other branches of topology, including differential topology, geometric topology, and algebraic topology.","description":"Branch of topology","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Algebraic topology
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":38801,"ns":0,"title":"Algebraic topology","extract":"Algebraic topology is a branch of mathematics that uses tools from abstract algebra to study topological spaces. The basic goal is to find algebraic invariants that classify topological spaces up to homeomorphism, though usually most classify up to homotopy equivalence.","description":"Branch of mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Complex analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":5759,"ns":0,"title":"Complex analysis","extract":"Complex analysis, traditionally known as the theory of functions of a complex variable, is the branch of mathematical analysis that studies complex-valued functions of one or more complex variables. It is used in many branches of mathematics, including functional analysis, algebraic geometry, number theory, analytic combinatorics, and applied mathematics, as well as in physics, including the branches of hydrodynamics, thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, and twistor theory.","description":"Branch of mathematics studying functions of a complex variable","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Functional analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":11180,"ns":0,"title":"Functional analysis","extract":"Functional analysis is a branch of mathematical analysis, the core of which is formed by the study of vector spaces endowed with some kind of limit-related structure (for example, inner product, norm, or topology) and the linear functions defined on these spaces and suitably respecting these structures. The historical roots of functional analysis lie in the study of spaces of functions and the formulation of properties of transformations of functions such as the Fourier transform as transformations defining, for example, continuous or unitary operators between function spaces.","description":"Area of mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Measure (mathematics)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":19873,"ns":0,"title":"Measure (mathematics)","extract":"In mathematics, the concept of a measure is a generalization and formalization of geometrical measures (length, area, volume) and other common notions, such as magnitude, mass, and probability of events. These seemingly distinct concepts have many similarities and can often be treated together in a single mathematical context.","description":"Generalization of mass, length, area and volume","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Combinatorics
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":5170,"ns":0,"title":"Combinatorics","extract":"Combinatorics is an area of mathematics primarily concerned with counting, both as a means and as an end to obtaining results, and certain properties of finite structures. It is closely related to many other areas of mathematics and has many applications ranging from logic to statistical physics and from evolutionary biology to computer science.","description":"Branch of discrete mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Differential geometry
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":8625,"ns":0,"title":"Differential geometry","extract":"Differential geometry is a mathematical discipline that studies the geometry of smooth shapes and smooth spaces, otherwise known as smooth manifolds. It uses the techniques of vector calculus, linear algebra and multilinear algebra.","description":"Branch of mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Euclidean geometry
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":9417,"ns":0,"title":"Euclidean geometry","extract":"Euclidean geometry is a mathematical system attributed to Euclid, an ancient Greek mathematician, which he described in his textbook on geometry, Elements. Euclid's approach consists in assuming a small set of intuitively appealing axioms (postulates) and deducing many other propositions (theorems) from these.","description":"Mathematical model of the physical space","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Probability theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":23542,"ns":0,"title":"Probability theory","extract":"Probability theory or probability calculus is the branch of mathematics concerned with probability. Although there are several different probability interpretations, probability theory treats the concept in a rigorous mathematical manner by expressing it through a set of axioms.","description":"Branch of mathematics concerning probability","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Order theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":361924,"ns":0,"title":"Order theory","extract":"Order theory is a branch of mathematics that investigates the intuitive notion of order using binary relations. It provides a formal framework for describing statements such as \"this is less than that\" or \"this precedes that\".","description":"Branch of mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Mathematical logic
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":19636,"ns":0,"title":"Mathematical logic","extract":"Mathematical logic is the study of formal logic within mathematics. Major subareas include model theory, proof theory, set theory, and recursion theory (also known as computability theory).","description":"Subfield of mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Mathematical analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":48396,"ns":0,"title":"Mathematical analysis","extract":"Mathematical analysis is the branch of mathematics that studies functions, spaces, and operators through methods of approximation and convergence.  It grew out of calculus, especially the use of derivatives and integrals to study variable quantities, and in the 19th century its foundations were reformulated with greater rigor.","description":"Branch of mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Convergence space
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":66374616,"ns":0,"title":"Convergence space","extract":"In mathematics, a convergence space, also called a generalized convergence, is a set together with a relation called a convergence that satisfies certain properties relating elements of X with the family of filters on X.  Convergence spaces generalize the notions of convergence that are found in point-set topology, including metric convergence and uniform convergence.  Every topological space gives rise to a canonical convergence but there are convergences, known as non-topological convergences, that do not arise from any topological space.","description":"Generalization of the notion of convergence that is found in general topology","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Dynamical system
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":9087,"ns":0,"title":"Dynamical system","extract":"In mathematics, a dynamical system is a system in which a function describes the time dependence of a point in an ambient space, such as in a parametric curve. Examples include the mathematical models that describe the swinging of a clock pendulum, the flow of water in a pipe, the random motion of particles in the air, and the number of fish each springtime in a lake.","description":"Mathematical model of the time dependence of a point in space","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Numerical analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":21506,"ns":0,"title":"Numerical analysis","extract":"Numerical analysis is the study of algorithms for the problems of continuous mathematics.  These algorithms involve real or complex variables (in contrast to discrete mathematics), and typically use numerical approximation in addition to symbolic manipulation.","description":"Methods for numerical approximations","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Module (mathematics)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":276410,"ns":0,"title":"Module (mathematics)","extract":"In mathematics, a module is a generalization of the notion of vector space in which the field of scalars is replaced by a (not necessarily commutative) ring. The concept of a module also generalizes the notion of an abelian group, since the abelian groups are exactly the modules over the ring of integers.","description":"Generalization of vector spaces from fields to rings","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Prime number
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":23666,"ns":0,"title":"Prime number","extract":"A prime number (or a prime) is a natural number greater than 1 that is not a product of two smaller natural numbers. A natural number greater than 1 that is not prime is called a composite number.","description":"Number divisible only by 1 and itself","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Antoine's necklace
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":15067130,"ns":0,"title":"Antoine's necklace","extract":"In mathematics, Antoine's necklace is a topological embedding of the Cantor set in 3-dimensional Euclidean space, whose complement is not simply connected. It also serves as a counterexample to the claim that all Cantor spaces are ambiently homeomorphic to each other.","description":"Embedding of Cantor set in 3-dimensional Euclidean space","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Alexander's subbase lemma
English Wikipedia article: Calculus
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":5176,"ns":0,"title":"Calculus","extract":"Calculus is the branch of mathematics that studies continuous change, and is the principal precursor of modern mathematical analysis. Originally called infinitesimal calculus or the calculus of infinitesimals, it has two major branches, differential calculus and integral calculus.","description":"Branch of mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Finite model theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1773596,"ns":0,"title":"Finite model theory","extract":"Finite model theory is a subarea of model theory. Model theory is the branch of logic which deals with the relation between a formal language (syntax) and its interpretations (semantics).","description":"Branch of logic","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Condensed detachment
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2621799,"ns":0,"title":"Condensed detachment","extract":"Condensed detachment (Rule D) is a method of finding the most general possible conclusion given two formal logical statements.\nIt was developed by the Irish logician Carew Meredith in the 1950s and inspired by the work of Łukasiewicz.","description":"Method in formal logic","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Fourier analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":11659,"ns":0,"title":"Fourier analysis","extract":"In mathematics, the sciences, and engineering, Fourier analysis () is the study of the way general functions on the real line, circle, integers, finite cyclic group or general locally compact Abelian group may be represented or approximated by sums of  trigonometric functions or more conveniently, complex exponentials. Fourier analysis grew from the study of Fourier series, and is named after Joseph Fourier, who showed that representing a function as a sum of trigonometric functions greatly simplifies the study of heat transfer.","description":"Branch of mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Harmonic analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":14147,"ns":0,"title":"Harmonic analysis","extract":"Harmonic analysis is an area of mathematical analysis that emerged from the study of harmonic functions, and especially their boundary behavior. The methods of harmonic analysis decompose functions and related objects, such as measures, into components based on symmetries, scales, spectra, or oscillation.","description":"Area of mathematical analysis","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Homological algebra
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":139410,"ns":0,"title":"Homological algebra","extract":"Homological algebra is the branch of mathematics that studies homology in a general algebraic setting. It is a relatively young discipline, whose origins can be traced to investigations in combinatorial topology (a precursor to algebraic topology) and abstract algebra (theory of modules and syzygies) at the end of the 19th century, chiefly by Henri Poincaré and David Hilbert.","description":"Branch of mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Commutative algebra
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":245990,"ns":0,"title":"Commutative algebra","extract":"Commutative algebra, first known as ideal theory, is the branch of algebra that studies commutative rings, their ideals, and modules over such rings. Both algebraic geometry and algebraic number theory build on commutative algebra.","description":"Branch of algebra that studies commutative rings","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Convex geometry
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":4165882,"ns":0,"title":"Convex geometry","extract":"In mathematics, convex geometry is the branch of geometry studying convex sets, mainly in Euclidean space. Convex sets occur naturally in many areas: computational geometry, convex analysis, discrete geometry, functional analysis, geometry of numbers, integral geometry, linear programming, probability theory, game theory, etc.","description":"Branch of geometry","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Discrete mathematics
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":8492,"ns":0,"title":"Discrete mathematics","extract":"Discrete mathematics is the study of mathematical structures that can be considered \"discrete\" (in a way analogous to discrete variables, having a one-to-one correspondence (bijection) with natural numbers), rather than \"continuous\" (analogously to continuous functions). Objects studied in discrete mathematics include integers, graphs, and statements in logic.","description":"Study of discrete mathematical structures","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Ring theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":250424,"ns":0,"title":"Ring theory","extract":"In algebra, ring theory is the study of rings, algebraic structures in which addition and multiplication are defined and have similar properties to those operations defined for the integers. Ring theory studies the structure of rings; their representations, or, in different language, modules; special classes of rings (group rings, division rings, universal enveloping algebras); related structures like rngs; as well as an array of properties that prove to be of interest both within the theory itself and for its applications, such as homological properties and polynomial identities.","description":"Branch of algebra","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Number theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":21527,"ns":0,"title":"Number theory","extract":"Number theory is a branch of mathematics devoted primarily to the study of the integers and arithmetic functions. Number theorists study prime numbers as well as the properties of mathematical objects constructed from integers (for example, rational numbers), or defined as generalizations of the integers (for example, algebraic integers).","description":"Branch of pure mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Real analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":26478,"ns":0,"title":"Real analysis","extract":"Real analysis is the part of mathematical analysis, especially as taught in undergraduate and graduate courses, that develops calculus rigorously over the real numbers and Euclidean spaces. Introductory real analysis is sometimes called advanced calculus, and studies limits, continuity, compactness, differentiation, integration, and series.","description":"Mathematics of real numbers and real functions","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Combinatorial principles
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1588279,"ns":0,"title":"Combinatorial principles","extract":"In proving results in combinatorics several useful combinatorial rules or combinatorial principles are commonly recognized and used.\nThe rule of sum, rule of product, and inclusion–exclusion principle are often used for enumerative purposes.","description":"Methods used in combinatorics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Geometric analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":4325474,"ns":0,"title":"Geometric analysis","extract":"Geometric analysis is a mathematical discipline where tools from differential equations, especially elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs), are used to establish new results in differential geometry and differential topology. The use of linear elliptic PDEs dates at least as far back as Hodge theory.","description":"Field of higher mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Category (mathematics)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":53759,"ns":0,"title":"Category (mathematics)","extract":"In mathematics, a category (sometimes called an abstract category to distinguish it from a concrete category) is a collection of \"objects\" that are linked by \"arrows\". A category has two basic properties: the ability to compose the arrows associatively and the existence of an identity arrow for each object.","description":"Collection of objects and morphisms","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Constructive analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":239851,"ns":0,"title":"Constructive analysis","extract":"In mathematics, constructive analysis is mathematical analysis done according to some principles of constructive mathematics.","description":"Mathematical analysis","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Algebraic geometry and analytic geometry
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":630505,"ns":0,"title":"Algebraic geometry and analytic geometry","extract":"In mathematics, algebraic geometry and analytic geometry are two closely related subjects. While algebraic geometry studies algebraic varieties, analytic geometry deals with complex manifolds and the more general analytic spaces defined locally by the vanishing of analytic functions of several complex variables.","description":"Two closely related mathematical subjects","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Antieigenvalue theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":34551376,"ns":0,"title":"Antieigenvalue theory","extract":"In applied mathematics, antieigenvalue theory was developed by Karl Gustafson from 1966 to 1968. The theory is applicable to numerical analysis, wavelets, statistics, quantum mechanics, finance and optimization.","description":"Applied mathematical theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Arens–Fort space
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":8588347,"ns":0,"title":"Arens–Fort space","extract":"In mathematics, the Arens–Fort space is a special example in the theory of topological spaces, named for Richard Friederich Arens and M. K. Fort, Jr.","description":"Topological space","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Abel's irreducibility theorem
English Wikipedia article: Anderson–Kadec theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":58422881,"ns":0,"title":"Anderson–Kadec theorem","extract":"In mathematics, in the areas of topology and functional analysis, the Anderson–Kadec theorem states that any two infinite-dimensional, separable Banach spaces, or, more generally, Fréchet spaces, are homeomorphic as topological spaces. The theorem was proved by Mikhail Kadec (1966) and Richard Davis Anderson.","description":"All infinite-dimensional, separable Banach spaces are homeomorphic","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Amalgamation property
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":11092492,"ns":0,"title":"Amalgamation property","extract":"In the mathematical field of model theory, the amalgamation property is a property of collections of structures that guarantees, under certain conditions, that two structures in the collection can be regarded as substructures of a larger one.\nThis property plays a crucial role in Fraïssé's theorem, which characterises classes of finite structures that arise as\nages of countable homogeneous structures.","description":"Concept in model theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Analytic proof
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1007110,"ns":0,"title":"Analytic proof","extract":"In mathematics, an analytic proof is a proof of a theorem in analysis that only makes use of methods from analysis, and that does not predominantly make use of algebraic or geometrical methods.  The term was first used by Bernard Bolzano, who first provided a non-analytic proof of his intermediate value theorem and then, several years later provided a proof of the theorem that was free from intuitions concerning lines crossing each other at a point, and so he felt happy calling it analytic (Bolzano 1817).","description":"Fundamental theory of logical analysis","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Affine plank problem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":82746225,"ns":0,"title":"Affine plank problem","extract":"In mathematics, the affine plank problem is an open question in convex geometry posed by Thøger Bang in 1951 as a strengthening of Tarski's plank problem. It asks whether the sum of the relative widths of any collection of planks covering a convex body must be at least 1.","description":"Open problem in convex geometry","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Group (mathematics)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":19447,"ns":0,"title":"Group (mathematics)","extract":"In mathematics, a group is a set with an operation that combines any two elements of the set to produce a third element within the same set. The following conditions must hold: the operation is associative, it has an identity element, and every element of the set has an inverse element.","description":"Set with associative invertible operation","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Abstract Wiener space
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":6592746,"ns":0,"title":"Abstract Wiener space","extract":"The concept of an abstract Wiener space is a mathematical construction developed by Leonard Gross to understand the structure of Gaussian measures on infinite-dimensional spaces. The construction emphasizes the fundamental role played by the Cameron–Martin space.","description":"Mathematical construction relating to infinite-dimensional spaces","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Additive process
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":64384314,"ns":0,"title":"Additive process","extract":"An additive process, in probability theory, is a cadlag, continuous in probability stochastic process with independent increments.\nAn additive process is the generalization of a Lévy process (a Lévy process is an additive process with stationary increments).","description":"Cadlag in probability theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Computability theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":155414,"ns":0,"title":"Computability theory","extract":"Computability theory, also known as recursion theory, is a branch of mathematical logic, computer science, and the theory of computation that originated in the 1930s with the study of computable functions and Turing degrees. The field has since expanded to include the study of generalized computability and definability.","description":"Study of computable functions and Turing degrees","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Floquet theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2987843,"ns":0,"title":"Floquet theory","extract":"Given a system in which the forces are periodic—such as a pendulum under a periodic driving force, or an oscillating circuit driven by alternating current—the overall behavior of the system is not necessarily fully periodic. For instance, consider a child being pushed on a swing: although the motion is driven by regular, periodic pushes, the swing can gradually reach greater heights while still oscillating to and fro.","description":"Branch of ordinary differential equations","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Antimatroid
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":667063,"ns":0,"title":"Antimatroid","extract":"In mathematics, an antimatroid is a formal system that describes processes in which a set is built up by including elements one at a time, and in which an element, once available for inclusion, remains available until it is included. Antimatroids are commonly axiomatized in two equivalent ways, either as a set system modeling the possible states of such a process, or as a formal language modeling the different sequences in which elements may be included.","description":"Mathematical system of orderings or sets","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Representation theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":19378200,"ns":0,"title":"Representation theory","extract":"Representation theory is a branch of mathematics that studies abstract algebraic structures by representing their elements as linear transformations of vector spaces. In essence, a representation makes an abstract algebraic object more concrete by describing its elements by matrices and their algebraic operations (for example, matrix addition, matrix multiplication).","description":"Branch of mathematics that studies abstract algebraic structures","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Modular representation theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1110685,"ns":0,"title":"Modular representation theory","extract":"In mathematics, modular representation theory is the part of representation theory that studies linear representations of finite groups over fields of positive characteristic. As well as having applications to group theory, modular representations arise naturally in other branches of mathematics, such as algebraic geometry, number theory and combinatorics.","description":"Representation theory of finite groups over fields of positive characteristic","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Analytic subgroup theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":35708725,"ns":0,"title":"Analytic subgroup theorem","extract":"In mathematics, the analytic subgroup theorem is a significant result in modern transcendental number theory.  It may be seen as a generalisation of Baker's theorem on linear forms in logarithms.","description":"Term used in transcendental number theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Andreotti–Vesentini theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":34938611,"ns":0,"title":"Andreotti–Vesentini theorem","extract":"In mathematics, the Andreotti–Vesentini separation theorem, introduced by Aldo Andreotti and Edoardo Vesentini (1965, 1965b) states that certain cohomology groups of coherent sheaves are separated.","description":"Certain cohomology groups of coherent sheaves are separated","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Big-little-big lemma
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":63679224,"ns":0,"title":"Big-little-big lemma","extract":"In the mathematics of paper folding, the big-little-big lemma is a necessary condition for a crease pattern with specified mountain folds and valley folds to be able to be folded flat. It differs from Kawasaki's theorem, which characterizes the flat-foldable crease patterns in which a mountain-valley assignment has not yet been made.","description":"Theorem about origami","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Arithmetic progression
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":168389,"ns":0,"title":"Arithmetic progression","extract":"An arithmetic progression, arithmetic sequence or linear sequence is a sequence of numbers such that the difference from any succeeding term to its preceding term remains constant throughout the sequence. The constant difference is called common difference of that arithmetic progression.","description":"Sequence of equally spaced numbers","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Degeneracy (mathematics)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":232952,"ns":0,"title":"Degeneracy (mathematics)","extract":"In mathematics, a degenerate case is a limiting case of a class of objects which appears to be qualitatively different from (and usually simpler than) the rest of the class; \"degeneracy\" is the condition of being a degenerate case. A given class of objects may be defined by several different systems of equations in most scenarios, and these different systems of equations may lead to different degenerate cases, while characterizing the same non-degenerate cases.","description":"Limiting case which is different from the rest of the class","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Bachmann–Howard ordinal
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":12732453,"ns":0,"title":"Bachmann–Howard ordinal","extract":"In mathematics, the Bachmann–Howard ordinal (also known as the Howard ordinal, or Howard–Bachmann ordinal) is a large countable ordinal.\nIt is the proof-theoretic ordinal of several mathematical theories, such as  Kripke–Platek set theory (with the axiom of infinity) and the system CZF of constructive set theory.","description":"Large countable ordinal","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Noncommutative harmonic analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":24062542,"ns":0,"title":"Noncommutative harmonic analysis","extract":"In mathematics, noncommutative harmonic analysis is the field in which results from Fourier analysis are extended to topological groups that are not commutative. Since locally compact abelian groups have a well-understood theory, Pontryagin duality, which includes the basic structures of Fourier series and Fourier transforms, the major business of non-commutative harmonic analysis is usually taken to be the extension of the theory to all groups G that are locally compact.","description":"Application of Fourier analysis to non-abelian topological groups","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Abelian category
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":45063,"ns":0,"title":"Abelian category","extract":"In mathematics, an abelian category is a category in which morphisms and objects can be added and in which kernels and cokernels exist and have desirable properties.\nThe motivating prototypical example of an abelian category is the category of abelian groups, Ab.","description":"Category with direct sums and certain types of kernels and cokernels","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Absolute continuity
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":252670,"ns":0,"title":"Absolute continuity","extract":"In calculus and real analysis, absolute continuity is a regularity property of functions that is stronger than uniform continuity, and hence continuity. The notion of absolute continuity allows one to generalize the fundamental theorem of calculus, originally in the framework of Riemann integration, to Lebesgue integration.","description":"Form of continuity for functions","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Algebraic analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":20846707,"ns":0,"title":"Algebraic analysis","extract":"Algebraic analysis is an area of mathematics that deals with systems of linear partial differential equations by using sheaf theory and complex analysis to study properties and generalizations of functions such as hyperfunctions and microfunctions. Semantically, algebraic analysis is the application of algebraic operations on analytic quantities.","description":"Technique of studying linear partial differential equations","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Albertson index
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":81286122,"ns":0,"title":"Albertson index","extract":"The Albertson index (also known as irregularity or Albertson irregularity index) is a graph invariant that measures the irregularity of a graph by summing the imbalances of all its edges. It was introduced by Michael O. Albertson in 1997 as a single parameter to capture how \"non-regular\" a graph is.","description":"Graph invariant measuring irregularity","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Adomian decomposition method
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2155356,"ns":0,"title":"Adomian decomposition method","extract":"The Adomian decomposition method (ADM) is a semi-analytical method for solving ordinary and partial nonlinear differential equations.  The method was developed from the 1970s to the 1990s by George Adomian, chair of the Center for Applied Mathematics at the University of Georgia.","description":"Method for solving differential equations","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Admissible representation
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":11055227,"ns":0,"title":"Admissible representation","extract":"In mathematics, admissible representations are a well-behaved class of representations used in the representation theory of reductive Lie groups and locally compact totally disconnected groups. title: English Wikipedia article: Action-angle coordinates
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":5435566,"ns":0,"title":"Action-angle coordinates","extract":"In classical mechanics, action-angle variables are a set of canonical coordinates that are useful in characterizing the nature of commuting flows in integrable systems when the conserved energy level set is compact, and the commuting flows are complete. title: English Wikipedia article: Algebraically compact module
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":478346,"ns":0,"title":"Algebraically compact module","extract":"In mathematics, algebraically compact modules, also called pure-injective modules, are modules that have a certain \"nice\" property which allows the solution of infinite systems of equations in the module by finitary means. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":4688415,"ns":0,"title":"Block matrix pseudoinverse","extract":"In mathematics, a block matrix pseudoinverse is a formula for the pseudoinverse of a partitioned matrix. title: English Wikipedia article: Borel–Cantelli lemma
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":44987,"ns":0,"title":"Borel–Cantelli lemma","extract":"The Borel–Cantelli lemma is a result in measure theory. title: English Wikipedia article: Limiting case (mathematics)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":40400729,"ns":0,"title":"Limiting case (mathematics)","extract":"In mathematics, a limiting case of a mathematical object is a special case that arises when one or more components of the object take on their most extreme possible values. title: English Wikipedia article: Moment (statistics)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":32960532,"ns":0,"title":"Moment (statistics)","extract":"In statistics, the moments of a probability density function are measures related to the shape of the function's graph. The first moment is the expected value, the second central moment is the variance, the third standardized moment is the skewness, and the fourth standardized moment is the kurtosis.","description":"Measure of the shape of a probability distribution function","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Back-and-forth method
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2033586,"ns":0,"title":"Back-and-forth method","extract":"In mathematical logic, especially set theory and model theory, the back-and-forth method is a method for showing isomorphism between countably infinite structures satisfying specified conditions. In particular it can be used to prove that:\n\nany two countably infinite densely ordered sets (i.e., linearly ordered in such a way that between any two members there is another) without endpoints are isomorphic.","description":"Technique used in mathematical logic","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Bounded quantifier
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":5824808,"ns":0,"title":"Bounded quantifier","extract":"In the study of formal theories in mathematical logic, bounded quantifiers (also known as restricted quantifiers) are often included in a formal language in addition to the standard quantifiers \"∀\" and \"∃\". Bounded quantifiers differ from \"∀\" and \"∃\" in that bounded quantifiers restrict the range of the quantified variable.","description":"Logical quantification that ranges over a subset of the universe of discourse","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Admissible numbering
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2423078,"ns":0,"title":"Admissible numbering","extract":"In computability theory, admissible numberings are enumerations (numberings) of the set of partial computable functions that can be converted to and from the standard numbering of partial computable functions. These numberings are also called acceptable numberings and acceptable programming systems.","description":"Concept in computability theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Autocovariance
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1202314,"ns":0,"title":"Autocovariance","extract":"In probability theory and statistics, given a stochastic process, the autocovariance is a function that gives the covariance of the process with itself at pairs of time points. Autocovariance is closely related to the autocorrelation of the process in question.","description":"Concept in probability and statistics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Acyclic model
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":19544067,"ns":0,"title":"Acyclic model","extract":"In algebraic topology, a discipline within mathematics, the acyclic models theorem can be used to show that two homology theories are isomorphic. title: English Wikipedia article: Convex analysis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":3237201,"ns":0,"title":"Convex analysis","extract":"Convex analysis is the branch of mathematics that studies convex sets, convex functions, and their applications to optimization, functional analysis, variational analysis, convex geometry, economics, and related fields.  A set is convex if it contains every line segment joining two of its points.","description":"Mathematics of convex functions and sets","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

English Wikipedia article: Adjugate matrix
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":202840,"ns":0,"title":"Adjugate matrix","extract":"In linear algebra, the adjugate or classical adjoint adj(A) of a square matrix A is the transpose of its cofactor matrix. title: English Wikipedia article: Amplitwist
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":59921578,"ns":0,"title":"Amplitwist","extract":"In mathematics, the amplitwist is a concept created by Tristan Needham in the book Visual Complex Analysis (1997) to represent the derivative of a complex function visually.","description":"Concept used to represent a derivative","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Almost everywhere
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":44688,"ns":0,"title":"Almost everywhere","extract":"In measure theory (a branch of mathematical analysis), a property holds almost everywhere (sometimes abbreviated as a.e.) if the set for which the property does not hold is negligible in a technical sense. The notion of \"almost everywhere\" is a companion notion to the concept of measure zero, and is analogous to the notion of almost surely in probability theory.","description":"Everywhere except a set of measure zero","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Extremal combinatorics
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2675917,"ns":0,"title":"Extremal combinatorics","extract":"Extremal combinatorics is a field of combinatorics, which is itself a part of mathematics. Extremal combinatorics studies how large or how small a collection of finite objects (numbers, graphs, vectors, sets, etc.) can be, if it has to satisfy certain restrictions.","description":"Area of combinatorics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Bicircular matroid
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":13511620,"ns":0,"title":"Bicircular matroid","extract":"In the mathematical subject of matroid theory, the bicircular matroid of a graph G is the matroid B(G) whose points are the edges of G and whose independent sets are the edge sets of pseudoforests of G, that is, the edge sets in which each connected component contains at most one cycle.\nThe bicircular matroid was introduced by Simões-Pereira (1972) and explored further by Matthews (1977) and others.","description":"Abstraction of unicyclic subgraphs","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Pregeometry (model theory)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1359832,"ns":0,"title":"Pregeometry (model theory)","extract":"Pregeometry, and in full combinatorial pregeometry, are essentially synonyms for \"matroid\". They were introduced by Gian-Carlo Rota with the intention of providing a less \"ineffably cacophonous\" alternative term.","description":"Formulation of matroids using closure operators","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Projective differential geometry
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1242592,"ns":0,"title":"Projective differential geometry","extract":"In mathematics, projective differential geometry is the study of differential geometry, from the point of view of properties of mathematical objects such as functions, diffeomorphisms, and submanifolds, that are invariant under transformations of the projective group. This is a mixture of the approaches from Riemannian geometry of studying invariances, and of the Erlangen program of characterizing geometries according to their group symmetries.","description":"Geometry","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Almost surely
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":351908,"ns":0,"title":"Almost surely","extract":"In probability theory, an event is said to happen almost surely (sometimes abbreviated as a.s.) if it happens with probability 1 (with respect to the probability measure). In other words, the set of outcomes on which the event does not occur has probability 0, even though the set might not be empty.","description":"Probability saying","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Alexandrov topology
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":542198,"ns":0,"title":"Alexandrov topology","extract":"In general topology, an Alexandrov topology is a topology in which the intersection of an arbitrary family of open sets is open (while the definition of a topology only requires this for a finite family). Equivalently, an Alexandrov topology is one whose open sets are the upper sets for some preorder on the space.","description":"Type of topology in mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Algebraic differential equation
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":9501827,"ns":0,"title":"Algebraic differential equation","extract":"In mathematics, an algebraic differential equation is a differential equation that can be expressed by means of differential algebra. There are several such notions, according to the concept of differential algebra used.","description":"Class of differential equations expressible in differential algebra","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Complemented lattice
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":753521,"ns":0,"title":"Complemented lattice","extract":"In the mathematical discipline of order theory, a complemented lattice is a bounded lattice (with least element 0 and greatest element 1), in which every element a has a complement, i.e. an element b satisfying a ∨ b = 1 and a ∧ b = 0.","description":"Bound lattice in which every element has a complement","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Adaptive step size
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":8449246,"ns":0,"title":"Adaptive step size","extract":"In mathematics and numerical analysis,  an adaptive step size is used in some methods for the numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (including the special case of numerical integration) in order to control the errors of the method and to ensure stability properties such as A-stability. \nUsing an adaptive stepsize is of particular importance when there is a large variation in the size of the derivative.","description":"Method in mathematics and numerical analysis","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":321831,"ns":0,"title":"Abundant number","extract":"In number theory, an abundant number or excessive number is a positive integer for which the sum of its proper divisors is greater than the number. title: English Wikipedia article: Cantor space
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":352376,"ns":0,"title":"Cantor space","extract":"In mathematics, a Cantor space, named for Georg Cantor, is a topological abstraction of the classical Cantor set: a topological space is a Cantor space if it is homeomorphic to the Cantor set. title: English Wikipedia article: Artin–Verdier duality
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":33899975,"ns":0,"title":"Artin–Verdier duality","extract":"In mathematics, Artin–Verdier duality is a duality theorem for constructible abelian sheaves over the spectrum of a ring of algebraic numbers, introduced by Michael Artin and Jean-Louis Verdier (1964), that generalizes Tate duality.\nIt shows that, as far as etale (or flat) cohomology is concerned, the ring of integers in a number field behaves like a 3-dimensional mathematical object.","description":"Theorem in number theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":18017949,"ns":0,"title":"Atiyah–Segal completion theorem","extract":"The Atiyah–Segal completion theorem is a theorem in mathematics about equivariant K-theory in homotopy theory. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":19266946,"ns":0,"title":"Mathematical diagram","extract":"Mathematical diagrams, such as charts and graphs, are mainly designed to convey mathematical relationships—for example, comparisons over time.","description":"Visual representation of a mathematical relationship","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2732301,"ns":0,"title":"Boolean-valued model","extract":"In mathematical logic, a Boolean-valued model is a generalization of the ordinary Tarskian notion of structure from model theory. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":39286332,"ns":0,"title":"Almost ring","extract":"In mathematics, almost modules and almost rings are certain objects interpolating between  rings and their fields of fractions. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":648042,"ns":0,"title":"ADE classification","extract":"In mathematics, the ADE classification (originally A-D-E classifications) is a situation where certain kinds of objects are in correspondence with simply laced Dynkin diagrams. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1734292,"ns":0,"title":"Absolutely convex set","extract":"In mathematics, a subset C of a real or complex vector space is said to be absolutely convex or disked if it is convex and balanced (some people use the term \"circled\" instead of \"balanced\"), in which case it is called a disk. \nThe disked hull or the absolute convex hull of a set is the intersection of all disks containing that set.","description":"Convex and balanced set","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Affine space
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":298834,"ns":0,"title":"Affine space","extract":"In mathematics, an affine space is a geometric structure that generalizes some of the properties of Euclidean spaces in such a way that these are independent of the concepts of distance and measure of angles, keeping only the properties related to parallelism and ratio of lengths for parallel line segments. title: English Wikipedia article: Almost periodic function
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":405512,"ns":0,"title":"Almost periodic function","extract":"In mathematics, an almost periodic function is, loosely speaking, a function of a real variable that is periodic to within any desired level of accuracy, given suitably long, well-distributed \"almost-periods\". text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":41452559,"ns":0,"title":"Approximate tangent space","extract":"In geometric measure theory an approximate tangent space is a measure theoretic generalization of the concept of a tangent space for a differentiable manifold.","description":"Measure-theoretic generalization of the concept of a tangent space","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":33509133,"ns":0,"title":"Cutting sequence","extract":"In digital geometry, a cutting sequence is a sequence of symbols whose elements correspond to the individual grid lines crossed (\"cut\") as a curve crosses a square grid.\nSturmian words are a special case of cutting sequences where the curves are straight lines of irrational slope.","description":"Records individual grid lines crossed (\"cut\") as a curve crosses a square grid","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":32341736,"ns":0,"title":"Tau (mathematics)","extract":"The number τ ( ; spelled out as tau) is a mathematical constant, equal to 2π, that has been proposed as an alternative to π by various proponents, who argue that mathematical notation would be simpler, clearer or pedagogically preferable if formulas and quantities (including angles) were described in terms of τ instead of π. title: English Wikipedia article: Blaschke sum
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":65158329,"ns":0,"title":"Blaschke sum","extract":"In convex geometry and the geometry of convex polytopes, the Blaschke sum of two polytopes is a polytope that has a facet parallel to each facet of the two given polytopes, with the same measure. When both polytopes have parallel facets, the measure of the corresponding facet in the Blaschke sum is the sum of the measures from the two given polytopes.","description":"Polytope combining two smaller polytopes","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Additive inverse
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":228312,"ns":0,"title":"Additive inverse","extract":"In mathematics, the additive inverse of an element x, denoted −x, is the element that when added to x, yields the additive identity. This additive identity is often the number 0 (zero), but it can also refer to a more generalized zero element.","description":"Number that, when added to the original number, yields the additive identity","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Amitsur–Levitzki theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":30373123,"ns":0,"title":"Amitsur–Levitzki theorem","extract":"In algebra, the Amitsur–Levitzki theorem states that the algebra of n × n matrices over a commutative ring satisfies a certain identity of degree 2n. It was proved by Amitsur and  Levitsky (1950).","description":"States that the algebra of n by n matrices satisfies a certain identity of degree 2n","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Alexandroff extension
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":55611,"ns":0,"title":"Alexandroff extension","extract":"In the mathematical field of topology, the Alexandroff extension is a way to extend a noncompact topological space by adjoining a single point in such a way that the resulting space is compact.  It is named after the Russian mathematician Pavel Alexandroff.","description":"Way to extend a non-compact topological space","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Absolute neighborhood retract
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":81809195,"ns":0,"title":"Absolute neighborhood retract","extract":"In mathematics, especially algebraic topology, an absolute neighborhood retract (or ANR) is a \"nice\" topological space that is considered in homotopy theory; more specifically, in the theory of retracts.\nFor a more general introduction to ANRs, see also Retraction (topology)#Absolute neighborhood retract (ANR).","description":"Math concept","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Antiholomorphic function
English Wikipedia article: Atom (measure theory)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":3058373,"ns":0,"title":"Atom (measure theory)","extract":"In mathematics, more precisely in measure theory, an atom is a measurable set that has positive measure and contains no set of smaller positive measures. A measure that has no atoms is called non-atomic or atomless.","description":"Minimal measurable set with positive measure","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Calculus on finite weighted graphs
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":61556353,"ns":0,"title":"Calculus on finite weighted graphs","extract":"In mathematics, calculus on finite weighted graphs is a discrete calculus for functions whose domain is the vertex set of a graph with a finite number of vertices and weights associated to the edges. This involves formulating discrete operators on graphs which are analogous to differential operators in calculus, such as graph Laplacians (or discrete Laplace operators) as discrete versions of the Laplacian, and using these operators to formulate differential equations, difference equations, or variational models on graphs which can be interpreted as discrete versions of partial differential equations or continuum variational models.","description":"Type of discrete calculus","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: ∞-Chern–Simons theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":79416318,"ns":0,"title":"∞-Chern–Simons theory","extract":"In mathematics, ∞-Chern–Simons theory (not to be confused with infinite-dimensional Chern–Simons theory) is a generalized formulation of Chern–Simons theory from differential geometry using the formalism of higher category theory, which in particular studies ∞-categories. It is obtained by taking general abstract analogs of all involved concepts defined in any cohesive ∞-topos, for example that of smooth ∞-groupoids.","description":"Combination of higher category theory with Chern–Simons theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Congruence lattice problem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":9755564,"ns":0,"title":"Congruence lattice problem","extract":"In mathematics, the congruence lattice problem asks whether every algebraic distributive lattice is isomorphic to the congruence lattice of some other lattice. The problem was posed by Robert P. Dilworth, and for many years it was one of the most famous and long-standing open problems in lattice theory; it had a deep impact on the development of lattice theory itself.","description":"Important problem in lattice theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Ambient isotopy
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":7404467,"ns":0,"title":"Ambient isotopy","extract":"In the mathematical subject of topology, an ambient isotopy, also called an h-isotopy, is a kind of continuous distortion of an ambient space, for example a manifold, taking a submanifold to another submanifold. For example in knot theory, one considers two knots the same if one can distort one knot into the other without breaking it.","description":"Concept in topology","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: A¹ homotopy theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":17346948,"ns":0,"title":"A¹ homotopy theory","extract":"In algebraic geometry and algebraic topology, branches of mathematics, A1 homotopy theory or motivic homotopy theory is a way to apply the techniques of algebraic topology, specifically homotopy, to algebraic varieties and, more generally, to schemes.  The theory is due to Fabien Morel and Vladimir Voevodsky.","description":"Application of homotopy to algebraic varieties","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Affine Lie algebra
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1350865,"ns":0,"title":"Affine Lie algebra","extract":"In mathematics, an affine Lie algebra is an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra that is constructed in a canonical fashion out of a finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra. Given an affine Lie algebra, one can also form the associated affine Kac-Moody algebra, as described below.","description":"Type of Kac–Moody algebras","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Andronov–Pontryagin criterion
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":20781979,"ns":0,"title":"Andronov–Pontryagin criterion","extract":"The Andronov–Pontryagin criterion is a necessary and sufficient condition for the stability of dynamical systems in the plane. It was derived by Aleksandr Andronov and Lev Pontryagin in 1937.","description":"Mathematics concept","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Affine arithmetic
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2244916,"ns":0,"title":"Affine arithmetic","extract":"Affine arithmetic (AA) is a model for self-validated numerical analysis.  In AA, the quantities of interest are represented as affine combinations (affine forms) of certain primitive variables, which stand for sources of uncertainty in the data or approximations made during the computation.","description":"Concept in mathematics","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Alexander polynomial
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1107647,"ns":0,"title":"Alexander polynomial","extract":"In mathematics, the Alexander polynomial is a knot invariant which assigns a polynomial with integer coefficients to each knot type. James Waddell Alexander II discovered this, the first knot polynomial, in 1923.","description":"Knot invariant","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Banach fixed-point theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":46676,"ns":0,"title":"Banach fixed-point theorem","extract":"In mathematics, the Banach fixed-point theorem (also known as the contraction mapping theorem or contractive mapping theorem or Banach–Caccioppoli theorem) is an important tool in the theory of metric spaces; it guarantees the existence and uniqueness of fixed points of certain self-maps of metric spaces and provides a constructive method to find those fixed points. It can be understood as an abstract formulation of Picard's method of successive approximations.","description":"Theorem about metric spaces","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Davenport–Schinzel sequence
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":20232529,"ns":0,"title":"Davenport–Schinzel sequence","extract":"In combinatorics, a Davenport–Schinzel sequence is a sequence of symbols in which the number of times any two symbols may appear in alternation is limited. The maximum possible length of a Davenport–Schinzel sequence is bounded by the number of its distinct symbols multiplied by a small but nonconstant factor that depends on the number of alternations that are allowed.","description":"Sequence with limited alternation of symbols","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Turn (angle)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":855329,"ns":0,"title":"Turn (angle)","extract":"The turn (symbol tr or pla) is a unit of plane angle measurement that is the measure of a complete angle—the angle subtended by a complete circle at its center. One turn is equal to 2π radians, 360 degrees or 400 gradians.","description":"Unit of plane angle where a full circle equals 1","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Analytical hierarchy
English Wikipedia article: Bessel function
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":4700,"ns":0,"title":"Bessel function","extract":"Bessel functions are a class of special functions that commonly appear in problems involving wave motion, heat conduction, and other physical phenomena with circular or cylindrical symmetry. They are named after the German astronomer and mathematician Friedrich Bessel, who studied them systematically in 1824.","description":"Family of solutions to related differential equations","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Ahlfors finiteness theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":30979615,"ns":0,"title":"Ahlfors finiteness theorem","extract":"In the mathematical theory of Kleinian groups, the Ahlfors finiteness theorem describes the quotient of the domain of discontinuity by a finitely generated Kleinian group. The theorem was proved by Lars Ahlfors, apart from a gap that was filled by Greenberg.","description":"Mathematical theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":332229,"ns":0,"title":"Additive group","extract":"An additive group is a group of which the group operation is to be thought of as addition in some sense.  It is usually abelian, and typically written using the symbol + for its binary operation.","description":"Group with an addition as its operation","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Appert topology
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":29057063,"ns":0,"title":"Appert topology","extract":"In general topology, a branch of mathematics, the Appert topology, named for Antoine Appert (1934), is a topology on the set X = {1, 2, 3, ...} of positive integers.\nIn the Appert topology, the open sets are those that do not contain 1, and those that asymptotically contain almost every positive integer.","description":"Example of a topology on the set of positive integers","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Abstract polytope
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1211056,"ns":0,"title":"Abstract polytope","extract":"In mathematics, an abstract polytope is an algebraic partially ordered set which captures certain combinatorial properties of a traditional polytope without specifying purely geometric properties such as the position of vertices.\nA geometric polytope is said to be a realization of an abstract polytope in some real n-dimensional space, typically Euclidean.","description":"Poset representing certain properties of a polytope","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Aubin–Lions lemma
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":14703145,"ns":0,"title":"Aubin–Lions lemma","extract":"In mathematics, the Aubin–Lions lemma (or theorem) is the result in the theory of Sobolev spaces of Banach space-valued functions, which provides a compactness criterion that is useful in the study of nonlinear evolutionary partial differential equations. Typically, to prove the existence of solutions one first constructs approximate solutions (for example, by a Galerkin method or by mollification of the equation), then uses the compactness lemma to show that there is a convergent subsequence of approximate solutions whose limit is a solution.","description":"Mathematical result in the theory of Sobolev spaces","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Ambient space (mathematics)
English Wikipedia article: ∞-Chern–Weil theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":79416340,"ns":0,"title":"∞-Chern–Weil theory","extract":"In mathematics, ∞-Chern–Weil theory is a generalized formulation of Chern–Weil theory from differential geometry using the formalism of higher category theory. The theory is named after Shiing-Shen Chern and André Weil, who first constructed the Chern–Weil homomorphism in the 1940s, although the generalization was not developed by them.","description":"Combination of higher category theory with Chern–Weil theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Beckman–Quarles theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":7580572,"ns":0,"title":"Beckman–Quarles theorem","extract":"In geometry, the Beckman–Quarles theorem states that if a transformation of the Euclidean plane or a higher-dimensional Euclidean space preserves unit distances, then it preserves all Euclidean distances. Equivalently, every homomorphism from the unit distance graph of the plane to itself must be an isometry of the plane.","description":"Unit-distance-preserving maps are isometries","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Blackwell-Girshick equation
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":74025273,"ns":0,"title":"Blackwell-Girshick equation","extract":"The Blackwell-Girshick equation is an equation in probability theory that allows for the calculation of the variance of random sums of random variables. It is the equivalent of Wald's lemma for the expectation of composite distributions.","description":"Variance of random sum","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Boolean differential calculus
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":55539147,"ns":0,"title":"Boolean differential calculus","extract":"Boolean differential calculus (BDC) (German: Boolescher Differentialkalkül (BDK)) is a subject field of Boolean algebra discussing changes of Boolean variables and Boolean functions.\nBoolean differential calculus concepts are analogous to those of classical differential calculus, notably studying the changes in functions and variables with respect to each other.","description":"Subject field of Boolean algebra discussing changes of Boolean variables and functions","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Abstract logic
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":28877379,"ns":0,"title":"Abstract logic","extract":"In mathematical logic, an abstract logic is a formal system consisting of a class of sentences and a satisfaction relation with specific properties related to occurrence, expansion, isomorphism, renaming and quantification.\nBased on Lindström's characterization, first-order logic is, up to equivalence, the only abstract logic that is countably compact and has Löwenheim number ω.","description":"Formal system in mathematical logic","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Affine symmetric group
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":67465897,"ns":0,"title":"Affine symmetric group","extract":"The affine symmetric groups are a family of mathematical structures that describe the symmetries of the number line and the regular triangular tiling of the plane, as well as related higher-dimensional objects. In addition to this geometric description, the affine symmetric groups may be defined in other ways: as collections of permutations (rearrangements) of the integers (..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ...) that are periodic in a certain sense, or in purely algebraic terms as a group with certain generators and relations.","description":"Number line and triangular tiling's symmetry mathematical structure","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Anosov diffeomorphism
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2320078,"ns":0,"title":"Anosov diffeomorphism","extract":"In mathematics, more particularly in the fields of dynamical systems and geometric topology, an Anosov map on a manifold M is a certain type of mapping, from M to itself, with rather clearly marked local directions of \"expansion\" and \"contraction\". Anosov systems are a special case of Axiom A systems.","description":"Diffeomorphism that has a hyperbolic structure on the tangent bundle","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Beauville–Laszlo theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":16829511,"ns":0,"title":"Beauville–Laszlo theorem","extract":"In mathematics, the Beauville–Laszlo theorem is a result in commutative algebra and algebraic geometry that allows one to \"glue\" two sheaves over an infinitesimal neighborhood of a point on an algebraic curve.  It was proved by Arnaud Beauville and Yves Laszlo (1995).","description":"Lets one glue 2 sheaves over an infinitesimal neighborhood of an algebraic curve point","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Almost perfect number
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":322008,"ns":0,"title":"Almost perfect number","extract":"In mathematics, an almost perfect number (sometimes also called slightly defective or least deficient number) is a natural number n such that the sum of all divisors of n (the sum-of-divisors function σ(n)) is equal to 2n − 1, the sum of all proper divisors of n, s(n) = σ(n) − n, then being equal to n − 1. The only known almost perfect numbers are powers of 2 with non-negative exponents (sequence A000079 in the OEIS).","description":"Numbers whose sum of divisors is twice the number minus 1","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Category of manifolds
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":10059981,"ns":0,"title":"Category of manifolds","extract":"In mathematics, the category of manifolds, often denoted Manp, is the category whose objects are manifolds of smoothness class Cp and whose morphisms are p-times continuously differentiable maps. This forms a category because the composition of two Cp maps is again continuous and of class Cp.","description":"Category whose objects are manifolds and whose morphisms are differentiable maps","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Dieudonné plank
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":34995146,"ns":0,"title":"Dieudonné plank","extract":"In mathematics, the Dieudonné plank is a specific topological space introduced by Dieudonné (1944). It is an example of a metacompact space that is not paracompact.","description":"Example of a metacompact topological space that is not paracompact","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Bing metrization theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":9712648,"ns":0,"title":"Bing metrization theorem","extract":"In topology, the Bing metrization theorem, named after R. H. Bing, characterizes when a topological space is metrizable.","description":"Characterizes when a topological space is metrizable","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Dehn's lemma
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":4362183,"ns":0,"title":"Dehn's lemma","extract":"In mathematics, Dehn's lemma asserts that a piecewise-linear map of a disk into a 3-manifold, with the map's singularity set in the disk's interior, implies the existence of another piecewise-linear map of the disk which is an embedding and is identical to the original on the boundary of the disk.\nThis theorem was thought to be proven by Max Dehn (1910), but  Hellmuth Kneser (1929, page 260) found a gap in the proof.","description":"Theorem in topology","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Bendixson–Dulac theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":634543,"ns":0,"title":"Bendixson–Dulac theorem","extract":"In mathematics, the Bendixson–Dulac theorem is a theorem in dynamical systems that exclude the existence of periodic orbits of two-dimensional flows. title: English Wikipedia article: Bing's recognition theorem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":15894497,"ns":0,"title":"Bing's recognition theorem","extract":"In topology, a branch of mathematics, Bing's recognition theorem, named for R. title: English Wikipedia article: Geometric progression
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":23474670,"ns":0,"title":"Geometric progression","extract":"A geometric progression, also known as a geometric sequence, is a mathematical sequence of non-zero numbers where each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous one by a fixed number called the common ratio. title: English Wikipedia article: Curry–Howard correspondence
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":254299,"ns":0,"title":"Curry–Howard correspondence","extract":"In programming language theory and proof theory, the Curry–Howard correspondence is a direct relationship between computer programs and mathematical proofs. title: English Wikipedia article: Arithmetical set
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2342451,"ns":0,"title":"Arithmetical set","extract":"In mathematical logic, an arithmetical set (or arithmetic set) is a set of natural numbers that can be defined by a formula of first-order Peano arithmetic. title: English Wikipedia article: André–Quillen cohomology
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":23974317,"ns":0,"title":"André–Quillen cohomology","extract":"In commutative algebra and algebraic geometry, André–Quillen cohomology is a cohomology theory for commutative rings and their modules, constructed using the cotangent complex. title: English Wikipedia article: Affine group
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":298828,"ns":0,"title":"Affine group","extract":"In mathematics, the affine group or general affine group of any affine space is the group of all invertible affine transformations from the space into itself. title: English Wikipedia article: Algebraic structure
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":106364,"ns":0,"title":"Algebraic structure","extract":"In mathematics, an algebraic structure or algebraic system consists of a nonempty set A (called the underlying set, carrier set or domain), a collection of operations on A (typically binary operations such as addition and multiplication), and a finite set of identities (known as axioms) that these operations must satisfy.\nAn algebraic structure may be based on other algebraic structures with operations and axioms involving several structures.","description":"Set with operations obeying given axioms","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Axiomatic foundations of topological spaces
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2123123,"ns":0,"title":"Axiomatic foundations of topological spaces","extract":"In the mathematical field of topology, a topological space is usually defined by declaring its open sets. title: English Wikipedia article: Abel's summation formula
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":9747155,"ns":0,"title":"Abel's summation formula","extract":"In mathematics, Abel's summation formula, introduced by Niels Henrik Abel, is intensively used in analytic number theory and the study of special functions to compute series.","description":"Integration by parts version of Abel's method for summation by parts","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Approximately continuous function
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":78828472,"ns":0,"title":"Approximately continuous function","extract":"In mathematics, particularly in mathematical analysis and measure theory, an approximately continuous function is a concept that generalizes the notion of continuous functions by replacing the ordinary limit with an approximate limit. title: English Wikipedia article: Asymptotic expansion
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":642090,"ns":0,"title":"Asymptotic expansion","extract":"In mathematics, an asymptotic expansion, asymptotic series, or Poincaré expansion is a formal series used to approximate a given function  near a specific point or at infinity. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":13505688,"ns":0,"title":"Analytic semigroup","extract":"In mathematics, an analytic semigroup is particular kind of strongly continuous semigroup.
